tail.title: A 2.6B Liquid coder is fine-tuned on 2,500 DeepSeek-V4 reasoning traces and ships GGUF alongside the safetensors
tail.summary: Built on LiquidAI/LFM2.5-2.6B through Unsloth using the Banaxi-Tech/Deepseek-V4-Reasoning-Code-2500 dataset, aimed at step-by-step code reasoning without losing general utility. The repo ships FP16/BF16 safetensors plus a Q4_K_M GGUF in the same tree, so it runs locally with no conversion step. No benchmark numbers are published, which is the standard gap in this class of small distills: the training-data provenance is the only evidence on offer.

tail.title: LMCache tags v0.5.4rc4 with prebuilt wheels for CUDA 12.9, CUDA 13.0 and AMD ROCm gfx942/gfx950
tail.summary: The ROCm 7.2 wheel targets AMD Instinct gfx942 (MI300X/MI325X) and gfx950 (MI350X/MI355X), ABI-matched to the upstream vllm/vllm-openai-rocm image at torch 2.11 and cp312, installable into an existing vLLM ROCm container with a single pip line. rc3 and rc4 both shipped inside 30 hours after an AMD release-pipeline CI failure was fixed. This is the release train carrying last week's CacheBlend work for Mamba2/GDN hybrids, which is the path that matters for the Nemotron and Qwen hybrid families.

tail.title: Atlas puts coding agents under source control: run several, track what each one changed, query them in one place
tail.summary: Treats agent runs as versioned artifacts rather than ephemeral sessions, so parallel agents working the same repo produce a diffable, attributable record instead of a merge mess. Patrick routinely fans out Opus subagents on heavy jobs; this is the missing layer that would let him see which subagent produced which change and roll one back without unpicking the rest.

tail.title: CONTINUUM checkpoints a long-running agent by meaning rather than by conversation, so recovery does not mean replaying the transcript
tail.summary: Writes verifiable semantic checkpoints during a run so an agent that dies or drifts can resume from a claimed state that can be checked, instead of from a rehydrated context window. The failure mode it targets is the one that eats Patrick's multi-hour research and eval runs, where a context compaction quietly loses the constraint the whole run depended on.

tail.title: A vibe-coding toolkit that bundles Claude Code plugins, subagent orchestration and quality gates as one opinionated set
tail.summary: Curated rather than exhaustive: the plugins, orchestration patterns and gate definitions the author actually kept after using them, packaged so you can install the set instead of assembling it. Worth reading against Patrick's own MCP/skill stack as a diff, specifically the quality gates, which is the part his pipelines mostly do by convention rather than enforcement.

tail.title: Vercel Labs ships deepsec, a security harness that drives coding agents at your codebase to find vulnerabilities
tail.summary: Rather than a scanner with a rule list, it structures coding agents into an adversarial sweep over your own repo and reports what they can actually reach. Patrick's audit work is methodologically the same move applied to models instead of code, and the harness design here, how you constrain an agent so its findings mean something, is the transferable part.

tail.title: The Astro creator brings React-style hooks to agent harnesses with Flue
tail.summary: Fred Schott's argument is that agent loops have the same state-and-effects problem React solved for UI, so a meta-harness should expose hooks rather than a config file: composable, testable units instead of one monolithic loop. Patrick writes a lot of bespoke orchestration; this is a genuinely different structural idea for it, not another wrapper CLI.

tail.title: Someone spent three months making desktop automation stop lying to AI agents
tail.summary: The premise is that most computer-use stacks return success for actions that silently did nothing, so the agent proceeds on a false world model; this one verifies that the click, type or focus change actually landed before reporting. Relevant to anyone running computer-use for real work, and a useful list of the specific ways the OS accessibility layer misreports state.

tail.title: n8n-skills teaches Claude Code to build n8n workflows that actually validate
tail.summary: A skillset encoding n8n's node schemas and connection rules so the agent stops emitting workflows that look right and fail on import. If Patrick ever wants NewsBrief's scheduling, Gmail hop and artifact publish wired as a visual pipeline he can hand to someone else, this is the shortest path from Claude Code to a working n8n graph.

tail.title: ComfyUI finally gets cable management for its spaghetti node graph
tail.summary: Daisy-chained links and PCB-style orthogonal routing so a workflow with 60 nodes stops looking like a hairball, applied to the existing graph without changing what it does. Purely quality-of-life, but it is the single biggest reason ComfyUI workflows become unmaintainable, and it is the rare custom node this month that is not another MiniMax-H3 wrapper.

tail.title: An RTX Video Super Resolution node for ComfyUI that runs on the NVIDIA driver's own upscaler
tail.summary: Wraps NVIDIA's driver-level RTX VSR as a workflow-compatible node with exact hybrid output sizing up to 16K, so upscaling costs GPU silicon rather than another diffusion pass. On a 16GB 5060 Ti that matters: Patrick can generate at a resolution that actually fits and let the hardware path do the enlargement instead of spending VRAM he does not have.

tail.title: Disney Research vectorizes line art by fitting 2D Gaussian splats to Bezier splines
tail.summary: Takes the splatting machinery everyone has been pointing at 3D scenes and aims it at a 2D problem, recovering clean editable spline curves from raster line art instead of a point cloud. The output is the thing an artist actually wants, vector paths, and it is a good illustration of a technique being ported sideways into a domain it was not built for.

tail.title: AI isn't outthinking mathematicians, it's out-remembering them
tail.summary: Reframes the recent run of AI mathematics results as retrieval and recombination over a literature no human can hold rather than novel reasoning, and argues that distinction changes what the benchmarks mean. A cleaner version of an argument Patrick's own audit work keeps running into: a system that looks like it reasoned may have looked it up.

tail.title: Secondhand book sales are booming, and the trade thinks AI is part of why
tail.summary: Booksellers describe readers deliberately reaching for objects with provenance, a physical copy with a history, as a reaction to not trusting what is new and generated. It is a demand-side signal about what publishing readers now want, which is a different and more useful thing than the usual supply-side AI-slop story.

tail.title: PC Gamer: the executives pushing AI-generated NPCs and writing are betting you cannot tell the difference
tail.summary: A working critique of what AI-written NPC dialogue actually costs a game, from people who play them, rather than a rights argument. Patrick is building a local-model AI-NPC mod for KCD2, so this is the sharpest available statement of what the player-side failure mode looks like and what his mod has to avoid being.

tail.title: The Xiaomi 17 Ultra photographed the eclipse and produced a sun where the moon was
tail.summary: The phone's scene-recognition AI decided it was looking at the moon, applied its moon enhancement, and returned a plausible photograph of something that was not there. A clean, physical demonstration of what generative enhancement does when its prior disagrees with the sensor, and the kind of failure that is invisible unless you happen to know what the sky looked like.

tail.title: A tech bro scraped Cara, the anti-AI photo app, then posted about it
tail.summary: Cara exists specifically as a place artists post work they do not want in training sets; someone scraped it and announced it as a demonstration that opting out is theatre. A culture moment worth having the details of, because the argument about whether platform-level opt-out means anything is going to keep arriving in Patrick's professional conversations.

tail.title: otophon is a plugin that plays tones inside your head
tail.summary: Uses binaural and psychoacoustic construction so the tone is generated by your auditory system rather than present in the signal, wrapped as a normal DAW plugin. A genuinely strange thing to have on a mixing bus, and a rare instance of a music tool built around a perceptual trick rather than a model.

tail.title: Twin robots that play guitar, and will work for tab
tail.summary: Two purpose-built machines, one fretting and one picking, driven from standard guitar tablature so the input format is something a human already writes. The engineering interest is in the fretting hand, which has to solve a real physical constraint problem per chord, and the whole thing is buildable rather than a lab piece.

tail.title: WASI-Env packs 90 suckless C binaries and SQLite3 into a single HTML file
tail.summary: One file you can open offline that contains a working Unix-ish userland compiled to WASI, including SQLite, with no server and no install. The practical use is handing someone a self-contained environment as an attachment; the impractical pleasure is that it is a whole operating environment inside a document.

tail.title: A quasicrystal animation playground that runs in WebXR
tail.summary: Interference patterns from summed plane waves, parameterised live, rendered in the browser and steppable into a headset. Pure visual mathematics with knobs, the sort of thing worth ten minutes when you want to look at something that is not text.

tail.title: The Art of CHIP-8: what people built inside a 4KB fantasy machine
tail.summary: A survey of the tricks CHIP-8 authors use to get expression out of 35 instructions, a monochrome 64x32 display and no sound beyond a beep. Constraint-driven creativity documented properly, and a good antidote to a week spent thinking about how many parameters something has.

tail.title: How 2004 RuneScape fit a multiplayer RPG down a 56k dial-up connection
tail.summary: Reverse-engineers the actual protocol: what got quantised, what got predicted client-side, and which visible game design choices exist because of a bandwidth budget. The recurring lesson is that severe constraints show up as aesthetics, which is why that game still looks like itself.

tail.title: Technology optimism hour
tail.summary: MacWright deliberately lists the things in software that have genuinely got better, as an exercise against a critical reflex he notices in himself and everyone he reads. Short, and unusually honest about the fact that it is a corrective rather than a belief.

tail.title: Foreman turns a coding agent into a build foreman that interviews you before it writes anything
tail.summary: A playbook that inverts the usual order: the agent runs a structured interview to extract requirements first, and only then plans and builds the site. The interview script is the reusable artifact here, since the questions it asks are the ones that stop a build from being rewritten twice.

tail.title: Val Town Access: one-click team-only auth for the internal tools you vibe-coded
tail.summary: Flips a switch to put a login in front of a val so an internal script stops being a public URL, which is the step almost everyone skips when a throwaway tool quietly becomes load-bearing. Relevant to Patrick's own habit of standing up small hosted utilities and then leaving them open.

tail.title: A local-inference rig's actual ComfyUI workflows and benchmark configs, published rather than described
tail.summary: The working files from a 4x RTX 3090 setup: the ComfyUI graphs that are actually run, plus the benchmark configs used to compare them, instead of a blog post about a rig. Even at a quarter of that VRAM the configs tell Patrick which settings the author tuned and why, which is faster than rediscovering the same knobs on a 5060 Ti.

tail.title: Could a computer scientist build a brain?
tail.summary: Takes the question literally and asks what specification a brain would need if you had to hand it to an engineer, then shows how much of neuroscience turns out to be description rather than spec. Sits exactly where Patrick's psychology background meets his model work, and it is an argument about what we do not know rather than another architecture analogy.

tail.title: Someone serves their website from a swarm of ESP32 microcontrollers sitting on a shelf
tail.summary: Real load balanced across a physical row of dollar microcontrollers, with the failure and recovery behaviour documented as the point rather than the caveat. The kind of build where the constraint is chosen for its own sake, and a reminder of how little compute a site actually needs.

tail.title: E3d-pilot is a repo-improving agent harness where nothing merges without a SHA gate
tail.summary: Runs agents continuously against a repository but makes every merge pass a commit-SHA-anchored gate, so a run cannot quietly land a change based on a stale tree it read an hour ago. The stale-read-then-write race is the specific way parallel agent setups corrupt a repo, and this is a concrete mechanism against it worth copying into Patrick's own fan-out runs.

tail.title: CLI-Anything wraps GUI software in a command line so agents can drive it
tail.summary: The bet is that the blocker for agents is not reasoning but interface: software built for humans exposes no callable surface, so this generates one and publishes the results to a shared hub. Where computer-use stacks fight the pixels, this converts the app into something an agent can call directly, which is the more durable answer if it holds up for the apps you actually use.

tail.title: Noema: AI needs public feedback at scale, and the mechanisms to collect it do not exist yet
tail.summary: Argues that the preference data steering frontier models comes from a narrow, paid, unrepresentative pool, and walks through what a genuinely broad public feedback mechanism would have to look like institutionally. This is Patrick's field written as policy rather than method, and it makes the sampling-frame argument his own demographic-bias audits make empirically.

tail.title: A Solitaire game small enough to load from a QR code
tail.summary: The entire playable game fits in the roughly 2.9KB a QR code can carry, so scanning the square is the download. A deliberate size-golf stunt in a week of hundred-gigabyte installs, and the write-up covers what had to be thrown away to get there.

tail.title: Zvi's breakdown of the Dwarkesh Patel / Ryan Greenblatt debate on recursive self-improvement
tail.summary: Zvi annotates the full podcast, which he frames as a debate about recursive self-improvement recorded in the light of the recent misalignment and hacking incidents at OpenAI, Anthropic and UK AISI. The core disagreement he draws out: Dwarkesh is AGI-pilled but not ASI-pilled because he believes models learn to do X only from examples of X and can then only do those Xs, whereas Greenblatt comes from Redwood's 'models be scheming' school. Zvi flags the 'aligned to whom?' section as the most frustrating stretch of the conversation.

tail.title: Metaphilosophy II: which empirical flywheels actually update your highest-level concepts
tail.summary: The second instalment argues philosophy is the process of updating the mind's highest-level concepts, and separates two complementary methods: drawing out contradictions and unifications among concepts you already hold, versus deliberately acquiring experiences likely to force an update. The awkward part it names directly is that you cannot choose which experiences to seek on the basis of a yet-higher concept, so the selection problem has no clean footing. It settles on mathematics and science as the study areas nearest our highest-level notions and works through how the epistemic flywheel runs in those domains.

tail.title: Free will is like temperature: a coarse-graining you only need because your model of the system is fuzzy
tail.summary: The argument is that free will occupies the same epistemic slot as temperature: if you knew every atom's position and velocity you could predict the gas exactly and the temperature would be a screened-off epiphenomenon, and the same substitution works for a person plus their environment. The payoff is that free will is a tool for building probability distributions over an agent's behaviour when your view of them is imperfect, not a metaphysical property, and two identically prepared people would have identical free will. Short, and useful mostly as a clean statement of a position that the author notes is in the water supply but rarely pointed at directly.

tail.title: A new interview series on Lean, formal methods and AI-assisted math formalization
tail.summary: Adi Baradwaj launches an interview series with people working in Lean, formal verification and math formalization, opening with Tanner Duve of Logical Intelligence, a Mathlib and CSLib contributor. The chaptered conversation covers AlgoLean, Turing incompleteness in Lean, Lean versus Rocq versus Haskell, and formal verification before and after AI at the 1:02 mark. Relevant if you care about whether autoformalisation is becoming a real verification route for AI-generated proofs rather than a demo.

tail.title: Ajeya Cotra scores her own ten 2026 AI forecasts five months early, and the math prediction is the one that broke
tail.summary: Cotra revisits ten qualitative predictions she made in mid-January across game play, logistics, video, game design and math, each with an 80% low-end and a 20% high-end task, and scores them as of 13 August. Her 50% time-horizon forecast on software tasks was already clearly too conservative by early March, and the prediction that AI would not land a paper in a top math journal fell (though more ambiguously than she assumed). The game-play low end was falsified twice over: Claude Opus 4.7 beat Pokemon Red in May in roughly 112,000 in-game steps, and Fable beat Pokemon FireRed in about 50 hours in June.

tail.title: Red-teaming GiveWell's eyeglasses cost-effectiveness model, and what falls out of the assumptions
tail.summary: Zach Gilfix works through GiveWell's 2024 'Eyeglasses for workers' cost-effectiveness analysis, which produced two estimates (15x and 11x cash) from two RCTs, both clearing the 2024 bar of 10x and the current bar of 6x by a wider margin. He then adds wrinkles the CEA does not carry, and flags the THRIVE RCT in rural Bangladesh (423 people with presbyopia) as one of the two load-bearing studies. The methodological point generalises past global health: this is a worked example of auditing a published cost-effectiveness model by counting the assumptions it needs rather than arguing with its conclusion.

tail.title: A space scientist's 100-hour case that satellite infrastructure is a viable AI takeover pathway on its own
tail.summary: JordanStone argues that space systems are unusually exposed: cybersecurity in the domain is weak, most space hardware will become legacy infrastructure faster than other industries during an intelligence explosion, and denial of space-surveillance data to one actor could move the global balance of power. He claims there is a fairly convincing story for AI taking over by manipulating elections, conflicts and stock markets through space systems alone, especially combined with superpersuasion. He is candid about provenance, over 100 hours of reading reports and papers, and notes AI helped draft the combined-attack-pathway scenario section.

tail.title: Fieldbuilding programmes should calibrate investment to value alignment, skill and context, not enthusiasm
tail.summary: Gergo proposes a 'calibration line' for talent programmes: resources should match an individual's potential for impact at a given moment, set by three factors, value alignment, skill level, and existing context in the field. He names both failure modes explicitly, overinvesting by putting intensive support behind poorly aligned or insufficiently skilled participants, and underinvesting by neglecting high-potential people. The complication he acknowledges is that most impact comes from the top 1-5% of graduates and you usually cannot identify them in advance.

tail.title: A pluralist account of moral progress, against the expanding-circle story
tail.summary: Rafael Ruiz's paper is out open-access in Ethical Theory and Moral Practice, arguing against the dominant 'expanding moral circle' picture in which moral progress just means extending concern to more beings. The paper is roughly half of chapter 2 of his PhD thesis and proposes a pluralist alternative in which inclusion is one mechanism among several. Worth a look if you are building fairness or moral-reasoning evaluations that quietly assume the expanding-circle model as ground truth.

tail.title: Debian is holding a two-week vote on LLM contributions with nine ballot options, from outright ban to climate-grounded discouragement
tail.summary: Debian opened a General Resolution vote on 15 August running to 28 August, with nine ballot options covering the full range: ban LLM contributions outright, allow them under disclosure and licensing conditions, permit AI only as an assistive tool while disallowing AI-generated direct contributions, or neither endorse nor prohibit and simply hold the existing quality bar. One option grounds the objection in ecological damage rather than provenance, and one is 'none of the above'. Only Debian Developers vote, by GPG-signed email, which makes this one of the few AI-provenance policies with an actual enfranchised electorate and a binding outcome rather than a position paper.

tail.title: A Connecticut plaintiff hid 3-point white-on-white prompt injections in court filings and lost e-filing privileges for it
tail.summary: The filings carried invisible instructions formatted as 3-point white text on a white background, aimed at any AI system that might review them. Judge Spader compared the attempt to secretly tampering with a jury and revoked the plaintiff's electronic filing privileges. Connecticut courts do not actually use AI to review filings, which is the interesting part: the sanction landed on intent alone, establishing that attempted prompt injection of a court is punishable whether or not a model was ever in the loop.

tail.title: PerceptionBench separates seeing from reasoning, and no frontier model clears 60%
tail.summary: Moonshot AI's PerceptionBench is built to isolate what multimodal models actually perceive from what they subsequently reason about, and no frontier model reaches 60% accuracy, with GPT-5.6 Sol leading by a narrow margin. The finding that matters for eval design is that many failures scored as reasoning errors in existing benchmarks in fact occur at the image-reading stage. That makes a large class of published multimodal reasoning results attribution-ambiguous unless perception was controlled separately.

tail.title: The 'tragedy of the cognitive commons': every firm that cuts junior roles is individually right and collectively erasing a profession's expertise
tail.summary: A new paper frames AI-driven elimination of entry-level work as a commons problem: each company benefits from cutting juniors, while the pipeline that produces the profession's senior expertise is a shared resource nobody has an incentive to maintain. The damage is structurally invisible in the short run because the missing cohort only shows up as absent experts. The paper puts the visible onset somewhere between 2030 and 2045, when today's uncreated junior roles would have matured into experienced practitioners.

tail.title: Building an AI text detector from scratch, then training a small model to defeat it
tail.summary: Prompted by Substack shipping an AI detector in its UI, Raschka implements a detector from scratch as a small-language-model project and then uses it as a verifier to train an SLM that produces text evading detection. The framing is deliberately adversarial: the point is to study the limits of AI detectors rather than to build a working one. It also doubles as a worked example of verifier-based LLM training applied to something other than math and code.

tail.title: Retraction Watch weekend reads: a self-described 'never AI' research firm was AI after all, and OpenAI's math breakthroughs don't add up
tail.summary: This week's roundup leads with the death of former Cambridge professor Jason Arday, who had been the subject of several recent Retraction Watch stories, then collects a research company that pitched itself as 'never AI' and turned out to be AI-generated, plus a piece arguing OpenAI's claimed math breakthroughs do not add up. The in-house week included a BMJ Group retraction of a COVID-vaccine mortality paper cited in a Senate hearing, and a biology journal pulling 100+ special-issue articles for peer-review manipulation. Useful as a standing scan of where AI provenance and peer-review integrity are actually colliding in the literature.

tail.title: Princeton student says she did not run the experiments described in her own retracted paper
tail.summary: Rishika Porandla's paper in Macromolecular Materials and Engineering has been retracted, and she states she did not conduct the experiments it describes. It follows Retraction Watch's earlier story treating the retraction as 'the starting point for a better study'. The case is a clean data point on how authorship attribution fails at the undergraduate end of the pipeline, which is where most reproduction attempts start.

tail.title: Working with AI feels more like leadership than coding, because the same prompt does not give the same result twice
tail.summary: Allen Bargi's argument is that the deterministic mental model people carry from programming is the wrong one, since identical prompts yield varied output, and the closer analogue is directing people. What follows practically is that the returns come from investing in clarity, context and feedback loops, sharing intent through examples and instructions, rather than from trying to force machine-like reproducibility. Short essay, and the useful part is that it names the specific expectation that breaks rather than gesturing at 'a new paradigm'.

tail.title: The AI situation in software development: the time did not vanish, it moved upstream
tail.summary: The post works through the practical choice between writing a detailed specification, making a high-level request, or something in between, and lands on the context window as the binding constraint: 'you can't just give a 3000-word, 4-page detailed dense spec and expect it to follow everything', so information has to be compressed strategically. The conclusion is that implementation time has not disappeared, it has shifted into upfront system design, changing assumptions and refining the dev setup. A grounded counterweight to productivity claims that only count the coding minutes.

tail.title: Aligning protein generative models to experimental data rather than sequence likelihood
tail.summary: The paper reports that conditioning protein generative models on experimental measurements, rather than training purely on sequence data, improves generative modelling quality. It is the same structural move as preference alignment in language models, substituting measured outcomes for the proxy objective the model was originally fit to. Worth reading as a transfer case for anyone thinking about grounding evaluation signals in something other than the training distribution.

tail.title: World Labs turns a single real robot demonstration into thousands of simulated training variations
tail.summary: World Labs' method takes one real-world robot task recording and generates thousands of simulated variants for training, attacking the data-scarcity bottleneck that keeps robot learning expensive. The evaluation question it raises is the familiar one for synthetic data: whether measured gains reflect genuine generalisation or the model learning the generator's own idiosyncrasies. Included here as a live instance of the synthetic-data validity problem outside of text.

tail.title: Effective altruism is not utilitarianism, and the conflation keeps costing the argument
tail.summary: James Brobin separates the two positions for a general audience: effective altruism is a commitment to spending a meaningful share of personal resources impartially and cost-effectively, while utilitarianism is a complete theory of what makes actions right. He puts numbers on the movement rather than the philosophy, over 300,000 lives saved over two decades and more than 10,000 people pledging 10% of income for life. Relevant mostly as a clean statement of a distinction that gets flattened whenever AI-risk funding gets criticised.

tail.title: All utilitarians should be classical utilitarians
tail.summary: James Brobin defends total hedonic utilitarianism in the Bentham and Mill sense, against each of the standard modifications, prompted by meeting twelve utilitarians of whom none held the classical view. He works through the alternatives one at a time, starting with the claim that goods other than happiness exist. A useful map of the modification space if you are building moral-reasoning evaluation items and need to know which positions are actually live.

tail.title: RMIT's mirror index is real but incomplete in the other direction, and each index omits listings the other carries
tail.summary: The standing rule since 14 August has been that RMIT runs a mirror path at /students/careers-opportunities/scholarships/research carrying listings the main /scholarships/research index does not show, which was established from two examples. The mirror index itself was swept in full today, roughly sixty research listings, and the picture is more awkward than the rule allowed. The mirror does carry listings the main index omits, including two not previously recorded here: 'PhD in human-centric cyber security for the project investigating designing and developing inclusive and intelligent cybersecurity literacy tools' and 'PhD Scholarship in Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning'. But the mirror also omits listings the main index carries, including both of the ones this board has been recommending — the PhD Scholarship in Trustworthy Large Language Models Through Test-Time Scaling and the culturally-inclusive-AI-safety listing. So neither index is a superset of the other and neither is an inventory. Both must be swept every run, and the absence of a listing from either one is not evidence it does not exist. The rest of the mirror's AI-adjacent inventory is weak for this profile: 'PhD Scholarship in Metaverse and Artificial Intelligence for Next Generation Educational Technology Platforms', 'PhD Scholarship in Generative AI for Intelligent Process Safety Management', 'PhD Scholarship in AI-driven fused RGB and hyperspectral vision for sorting waste plastics', and 'PhD Application for CSIRO iPhD – AI for Stroke Detection', which per the standing rule on CSIRO Industry PhD programmes should be assumed domestic-only until read. The two listings that matter at RMIT remain the Newn HCI project and the trustworthy-LLM project, both governed by the 30 August international EOI rather than by any date printed on their own pages.

tail.title: Coefficient's capability-evaluations RFP is closed to new expressions of interest, and yesterday's board listed it as open
tail.summary: Read directly for the first time through the same curl workaround. The Improving Capability Evaluations RFP now states 'The window to submit an expression of interest (EOI) has closed. We will review EOIs on a rolling basis and aim to respond within two weeks.' Reviewing continues for EOIs already filed; new ones are not being taken. The sibling Capacity-Building fund on the same parent page is genuinely open and genuinely individual-eligible: 'This includes applications from both organizations and individuals, and includes both full-time and part-time projects' and 'Applications are open until further notice and will be assessed on a rolling basis.' Two funds, two opposite states, one funder - which is exactly the pattern that makes aggregator rows unreliable here.

tail.title: Halcyon Futures runs career-transition grants up to $500K and publishes no eligibility criteria at all
tail.summary: New to this board via the aisafety.com funding index, which lists it at 'Up to $1M'. The funder's own page splits that into four instruments: 'Career transition support' with 'Grants up to $500K', 'Nonprofit seed grants' at 'Grants up to $1M', venture investments 'up to $1M, and sometimes much more', and incubations. No deadlines. Critically, the page states nothing about whether individuals can apply or whether international applicants are accepted - the only route in is a 'Request for Founders' form or hello@halcyonfutures.org. Recorded as unverified on individual eligibility, not as eligible. The framing throughout is founders and new organizations, which is a poor match for a solo auditor who is not trying to start an org.

tail.title: The UK AISI Alignment Project is closed and says it is unlikely to run again this year - one fewer large route to track
tail.summary: Verbatim: 'Applications for the Alignment Project are currently closed. We are unlikely to run a similar program in 2026, but AISI does expect to run further academic grant programs.' The 2025 round 'awarded grants ranging from GBP50,000 to GBP1,000,000'. The page never states whether unaffiliated individuals could apply, and the word 'academic' in the forward-looking sentence is the tell - the successor programmes are being signalled as academic grant programmes, which is the affiliation gate in its usual form. Logged as a closed route so it stops absorbing attention.

tail.title: AI-Native Academia is a NeurIPS workshop about who governs peer review under AI, and it closes on 29 August
tail.summary: New to this board. 'Aug 29, 2026' deadline, 'Short papers (4 pages) and long papers (9 pages), references excluded', non-archival, double-blind, and it explicitly takes work already under review elsewhere: 'Non-archival, under-reviewed NeurIPS papers can also be submitted.' Site is Atlanta, 'Dec 12-13, 2026', confirmed against the official NeurIPS roster where it does not appear in the Sydney 48. The programme convenes PC chairs of ICLR, ICML and CVPR to redesign 'authorship, peer review, citation, and conference governance under AI'. The scope is the sociology of ML publishing rather than model evaluation, so the fit depends on whether Patrick wants to argue about the review system itself. No fee or affiliation requirement stated - unverified, not absent.

tail.title: World Models for High-Stakes Health resolves to Atlanta and 1 September, and its tracker entry is nine hours earlier than its own page
tail.summary: Upgraded from a tracker-only row to a page read, closing a carry-forward. 'September 1, 2026, AoE', 'Full Papers: at most 9 pages of main text. Extended Abstracts: at most 4 pages of main text', 'The workshop is non-archival. Papers under review elsewhere are welcome', and site 'December 11-12, 2026 (Atlanta)' - so not Sydney, consistent with its absence from the official 48. One genuine discrepancy survives the AoE-to-UTC reconciliation: aiworkshoptracker gives 'Sep 1, 2026, 21:59 UTC', which is 09:59 AoE on 1 September, roughly fourteen hours EARLIER than the page's 1 September AoE. That is not the standard offset, so it is either a portal time or a tracker error. Work to the earlier time. Scope is clinical trial simulation, not clinical bias, so topical fit stays partial.

tail.title: The EA Infrastructure Fund is alive at /funds/ea-community and the path this board recorded as a stub is confirmed dead
tail.summary: Confirmed by page read via curl: the live Effective Altruism Infrastructure Fund page sits at /funds/ea-community and carries a working 'Apply for funding' route, while /funds/ea-infrastructure remains a stub. Same silent-rename pattern that turned the Long-Term Future Fund into the Transformative AI Fund without rebuilding the application URL, which still contains ?fund=Long-Term%20Future%20Fund. aisafety.com/funding lists 'Effective Altruism Infrastructure Fund | Rolling basis | Individuals Eligible: Yes' - the fund is real and the path is now verified, but the scope is EA movement infrastructure, meaning talent, capital and knowledge pipelines, not technical alignment research. A solo LLM-audit proposal is a poor fit here and belongs at the Transformative AI Fund instead.

deadlines.label: GovAI Research Scholar, Research Fellow and DC Chief of Staff close TONIGHT
deadlines.note: RE-VERIFIED ON SOURCE PAGE TODAY, final call. Verbatim: '23:59 Anywhere on Earth (AoE) on Sunday, 16 August 2026' for Research Scholar and Research Fellow; 'Sunday, August 16 at 11:59 p.m. ET' for DC Chief of Staff. AoE gives roughly another 24 hours from Australian time. Confidence high on dates, nil on feasibility.

deadlines.label: LASR Labs remote contract screening closes TODAY (GBP50/hr)
deadlines.note: RE-VERIFIED ON SOURCE PAGE TODAY rather than carried forward. Verbatim: 'August 16th, 2026' deadline, start 'September 2026', 'GBP50 per hour, negotiable based on experience', hours 'flexible, ideally at least 10 hours per week' across windows 'roughly 2 to 3 weeks, a few times per year', and 'remote'. Applications via an Airtable form linked from the page. ELIGIBLE FOR AN UNAFFILIATED APPLICANT: no degree, affiliation or residency requirement appears anywhere in the listing, and remote hourly contracting does not collide with the WHV six-month single-employer rule. This is the only paid remote contract role found across seven runs that publishes an hourly rate. Confidence high.

deadlines.label: AI Alignment Foundation Research Fellowship closes ($12,000, remote, work from anywhere)
deadlines.note: RE-VERIFIED ON SOURCE PAGE TODAY, upgrading a two-run carry-forward to a fresh read. Verbatim: 'Aug 17 (AoE)', '$12,000 For the full 8-week program, paid in installments', '8 weeks Full-time . 40 hrs/week', 'Remote Full-time, work from anywhere'. ELIGIBLE AND EXPLICITLY SO: the programme 'welcomes researchers at any career stage, including recent PhDs, MSc students, and those transitioning from other fields', and asks for 'prior independent research output (thesis, paper, LessWrong post, etc.)' - Patrick's three solo arXiv papers satisfy that outright. NEW DISQUALIFIER FOUND THIS RUN, and it is the reason to read the page rather than the aggregator: the fellowship states it is NOT suitable for applicants 'primarily interested in policy/governance-focused work' and requires 'hands-on experimental experience' with a 'strong ML background'. Patrick's audit pipelines are empirical, so this reads as a fit, but the framing of a submission has to be technical-experimental rather than methodological-critical. Full-time 40 hrs/week for 8 weeks is the real cost. Confidence high.

deadlines.label: Kairos SPAR Fall 2026 mentee applications close (unpaid, fully virtual)

Three hops, all 200, all read first-hand today. The instrument shows 'Closing date 31/12/2026', 'Status Open', 'Who is it for? Future PhD candidates, Australian Citizen, International Student, New Zealand Citizen, Permanent Resident', and verbatim 'Applications are now open to Australian or New Zealand citizens (domestic), Australian permanent residents (domestic), and International applicants - subject to the eligibility requirements outlined under each project' and 'PhD Project Scholarships are open for applications year-round... each project will be open until filled.' FEE-SPLIT: ONE DECISION, FAVOURABLE SHAPE — 'a Research Training Program (RTP) or La Trobe Graduate Research Scholarship (LTGRS) stipend for up to three and a half (3.5) years, with a value of $36,000 per annum (2026 rate)' AND 'a Research Training Program (RTP) Fees Offset scholarship or La Trobe Full Fee Research scholarship (LTUFFRS) for up to four years for a doctoral degree', plus relocation and thesis/publication allowances. Four years of fees against 3.5 of stipend. OSHC is NOT mentioned — unresolved, not negative. ELIGIBILITY VERDICT — THIS IS THE SINGLE BEST-WRITTEN CLAUSE FOR PATRICK'S FILE FOUND IN NINE RUNS, verbatim: 'In selecting successful applicants, we prioritise applications from candidates who... have completed a Masters by Research or other significant body of research, such as an honours research thesis or lead authorship of a peer-reviewed publication, assessed at a La Trobe Masters by research standard of 75 or above.' LEAD AUTHORSHIP OF A PUBLICATION IS NAMED AS A SUBSTITUTE FOR THE HONOURS THESIS ITSELF, not as supporting evidence for an equivalence case. Three solo first-author papers is exactly the shape of that sentence. TWO HONEST CATCHES. (1) 'peer-reviewed' — arXiv preprints are not, so the claim has to rest on what the papers are rather than where they sit, and this is the question to ask research.study@latrobe.edu.au. (2) It says 'we prioritise', not 'you must have', so it is a ranking preference, not a floor — which cuts both ways and is softer than a bar. HARD BLOCKER: 'contact the primary supervisor listed against the project, and receive their invitation to submit a full application' and 'Please do not submit your application through our online portal without an invitation from the primary supervisor, as your application will not be accepted without their support.' THE PROBLEM IS THE PROJECT LIST: it was read today and contains NO XAI, LLM, HCI or trust project. The only two AI-adjacent entries are 'PRO-25127 - Machine Learning-Driven Simulation of Synchrotron and XFEL Beamlines' and a flexible-pressure-sensor project mentioning human-machine interaction. La Trobe does host an AI Institute and the Australian Centre for Artificial Intelligence in Medical Innovation (ACAMI), so the move is to watch the project list, which updates continuously, rather than to apply now. Note also the separate RTP/LTGRS central round has NO published dates at all: 'Check back periodically for information on the application process, and open and closing dates... when they become available.' High confidence throughout, first-hand.

WHY IT LEADS THE NOMINATIONS DESPITE THE CONFIDENCE PROBLEM: this is the only funded Australian project found in nine runs where a PSYCHOLOGY background is an advertised asset rather than the thing that fails the H1 test, and its subject matter is Patrick's three papers almost line for line — LLM bias propagation, explanation quality, trust and over-reliance. No tuition statement, no OSHC statement and no honours bar were captured. THE ACTION IS AN EMAIL, NOT A FETCH, and it should go out inside the 16 days before Monash international R1 opens on 1 September, because that round is the vehicle a project like this is funded through.
